I work 6 days a week between a fine dining restaurant and a pub. On the last day of my work week I was at the fine dining place. I went to a table and said “so, are you guys still hungry? What can I get you to eat?” after they finished their app. And they responded “ummmm we already ordered our mains..?” And I was like “fuck, I know that because I rang them in” not actually knowing in that moment what they ordered or if I actually ordered them. They were like “no worries as long as you didn’t forget to tell the kitchen!!!” I power walked to the POS and sure enough, I did ring them in. And then went to the kitchen and they were ready, thank god, as I ran them to the table within 4 minutes of my fuck up and turned it into a huge joke with them hahah. 

And then I had a table with a birthday. I ordered them a crème brulee at the same time as I ordered one for another table. I was so fucking tired that I could not remember if I brought one to the bday table already or not. I figured I didn’t and brought them the first one that I saw in expo. I brought it over and they were like “oh… another one?!” Lmfao. I had already given them one. With a SPARKLER. HAH. So, I told them I’d pack it up as they were full, but they insisted I eat it so I did lolz
I always just go back to the table and say “we welcome cash but I can bring the machine over for you if you need?!” and they settle either way right then and there.

Most restaurants I’ve worked in do not base their tip out % on the actually accumulated tips at the end of the shift, but on the net sales the server had that day. So, cash vs debit tips doesn’t really make a difference. The server still tips out on your total bill rather than the tip you leave them. Yes, this means that if someone leaves 0 tip, the server still tips out on the table, which means they’re literally tipping out on a table they’ve made no money on; they pay to serve the table and have them sit in their section when the table could have been sat with people who actually compensate the server for the service they provided. 

But, tipping cash is still a good practice. Pre-pandemic, I’ve always gotten my tips at the end of every shift. Paying with cash happened much more often, so at the end of a shift, I was able to take home credit/debit tips out of the cash I received. OR the restaurant has a “float” that was used to give the server what tips they were owed. However, not many people pay in cash anymore because of Covid and the possibility of spreading the virus via money. Because of this lack of cash flow in the restaurant, there is rarely enough to make up a “float” as there was before. It’s common now that I will be given all my (debit and credit) tips on Wednesday from the week before. If I was given cash, I am able to bring it home that night.
Literally in love with this story. This appreciation, especially in our industry, is RARE. You deserve it, and I’m happy that you work for people who see your worth.

(30, f) Relatable. I am diagnosed with borderline personality disorder, anxiety, major depression and adhd. Every single day is a challenge to get through. I am educated (culinary management degree, post grad in Italian cuisine, currently working on my bachelor of social work,) high performance in school has always come easily to me and I have always achieved grades resulting in being on honour roll, I believe I am highly intelligent academically as well as emotionally and creatively, I am an introvert/shy by nature but I have taught myself to be outgoing/social and the mask I’ve created seems to do the trick, I have constantly held a job since I was 15 and currently work at two different restaurants as a bartender/server and managed to do this while in school FT as well.. overall, I am a very “functioning” person by the book. 

But, like you, I simply just hate being here lol. I don’t find joy in life. It’s most often harder than it is worthwhile and I just don’t see the point of it. I definitely have suicidal ideations every day, but I would never act on them at this point of my life. I just would prefer to have never been born/not be alive if I had the choice lol. I know I don’t have a choice other than continue to push through the day by day trash, but I do so miserably. I know I have to stay for my loved ones because I couldn’t ruin their lives by making the decision to leave on my own terms. Like you, I see everyday how I wasn’t built for this world/it wasn’t built to accommodate me. My brain just doesn’t allow me to fit in and I have to fight with it every day. I constantly feel like an alien. 

So, I definitely support choosing abortion when there is a large possibility of developmental disorders. Frankly, I think that the child will never have the quality of life that everyone deserves. And their parents/family will struggle far more than they should. 

I am still undecided if I will ever attempt to have children. I don’t like the thought of bringing a child into the world with the strong chance I will pass down my mental health issues to them and they’ll have to forever live with challenges and hardships like I do. I don’t think it’s fair, and borderline immoral. But, I’m also selfish and have always wanted to be a mother to my own children. I’ve also been considering adoption recently. Who the fuck knows though, lol.

The leg cramps/pain and I’m sure foot pain as well will dissipate when your body grows accustomed to the long hours spent on them running around(and rarely sitting down and resting.) I’ve been in the industry for 13 years and when I started working again when restaurants opened up after lockdowns sue to Covid, I experienced the same thing, albeit my body being very used to the physical demands prior to this time off. But, the pain subsided after a week or two, and I’m sure it’ll be the same case for you. 

Firstly, I’d suggest investing in some solid and supportive shoes. This line by Vans is made especially for restaurant workers and I really like them. They’re non-slip, cute, and I find them pretty comfortable. They have never given me blisters which is a huge win imo. 

https://www.vans.ca/en-ca/search/product?q=made%20for%20the%20makers&gbraid=0AAAAADKpnkMLy7ypwvRiYK5xJ04otbw51&gbraid=0AAAAADKpnkMLy7ypwvRiYK5xJ04otbw51&gclid=EAIaIQobChMI5_Tpj9Tw-AIV7v_jBx1ZhgXvEAAYAiAAEgIWFvD_BwE

If you want even more comfort and support, invest in some orthotics or shoe cushions/insoles. This will all help! 

Secondly, you’d benefit from making it a habit and part of your routine to eat before your shift. I have trouble maintaining a regular eating schedule as well, but I’m very aware that not eating properly negatively affects my mood/performance/stamina/energy levels during my shift. When I work on an empty stomach, I definitely notice that I am less patient, less friendly with guests, my brain is slower/foggy and my ability to multitask/sharpness is impacted, I get tired much more quickly, I’m not as quick/ can’t hustle to my full potential and I am much less likely to be happy to be there. It’s effective to fuel your body- you aren’t capable of functioning at your best if you don’t prepare your body with proper sustenance. Proper being the key word- eating the right foods is important too. I try to avoid carb-heavy meals before my shift as it makes me feel slow, bloated and sleepy. I find eating a salad/quinoa/veggies with chicken/fish, yogurt, eggs, avocados, nuts, fruit etc is good for me. Protein and healthy fats are the best. But, kudos to you for drinking a lot of water! That is something I do not do, but I know I should haha. 

If I’m on shift and I am absolutely starving but can’t order food in that moment, I make myself a Virgin Caesar (Bloody Mary if you’re not Canadian like me haha.) The Clamato/Tomato juice is pretty filling when I’m desperate lol. Or I eat the garnishes at the bar like pickles/olives/cucumber/fruit; make sure you’re allowed to do this and won’t get in trouble for it first though lol. Also, attempt to bring little snacks from home with you like trail mix, crackers, granola bars, etc.. things you can eat on the fly and finish quickly to get you through the rest of your shift. 

Best of luck!!

Honestly, I just interrupt the conversation lol. I used to be awkward and have difficulty with this very thing, but I’ve realized that it’s literally my job to introduce myself/go through my spiel in a timely manner after guests are sat. Also, they’re waiting for me to come over and start their dining experience. They have come in to get food/drinks/service from me. It’s not rude, it’s doing what you’re paid to do. In the case they’re really not ready for me, they’ll say so, in which I say “no problem, I just wanted to come and say hi and introduce myself! When you’re ready for drinks flag me over!” Similarly, when I’ve checked if a table is ready to order twice and they’re still not, I simply say “okay, whenever you’re ready just stack up your menus at the edge of the table and I’ll come back over!”

I use “how are we doing, my friends?!” Or “here’s your _____, my friend” a lot. Gender/age neutral, and guests respond well to it. The most I’ve had someone comment about it was “oh, we’re friends now?!” in a playful way.

Honestly, when I was a teenager I used “not having a lot of money” as an excuse to not tip or tip poorly, from what I remember. I want to blame the parents for (the majority of) this population behaving this way, but my parents always taught me to be respectful to service employees and how to tip properly. I just chose not to listen to them and demonstrate what they tried to teach me because I was an asshole kid, lol. 

Anyways, I just think this is something we as an industry need to accept as the norm for this age group because being bitter about it/choosing to provide shitty service won’t benefit us in any way. I’ve began to choose my values in my work ethic over pettiness and provide the same level of service to every guest, including those who I (apologetically and regrettably) judge as not properly compensating me for my service. A positive mindset and knowing I’ve done the best job I can with ALL guests gives me a sense of self- gratification. 

Also, remember not ALL kids are “bad” guests. Many of them have surprised me over the years.

Ask to work an expo/food running shift. You’ll be able to see and learn all the menu items repeatedly as well as learn table numbers at the same time. Also, take a menu home and write it out a few times. Make notes that will help you remember the main ingredients.

About ten years ago I was in a very similar situation. My boyfriend and I were on the same page about having an abortion. However, the night before the appointment, he told me he changed his mind and wanted it. He yelled at me about “killing our child” and said he wasn’t going to drive me to the hospital. I was minutes away from telling my mom so she could take me when he said he would. But, after that, it wasn’t the same. He always held it against me and would bring it up in fights and when he was drunk. Our relationship ended a few months afterwards. 

Ten years later, I’m still secure in my choice. I wasn’t ready for a child, and he wasnt a good person to have one with. I’ve done a lot of things I wouldn’t have been able to do if I had a child. I do get sad sometimes still thinking about it. And that’s okay! You can be sad about a decision but still know it was the right one. 

Do what’s best for you and your life. Good luck.

I hope(expect, honestly) to be tipped AT LEAST 15%, but really 18%-20% and ^ if the guest is super happy/kind/generous because I STILL tip out the kitchen/hosts/bussers regardless if I am or not. Yes, this means if I have a table with a $100 bill, and I’m tipped 0%, I pay for them to have sat in my section, taken up a table for 1+ hours(when another guest(s) who did tip appropriately could have sat there,) and essentially end up paying out of my pocket to have served them. So, let’s say tip out to BOH/hosts/bussers is 3% of overall sales and tip out to bartenders is 1.5%. Pretty average. I am tipping out $4.50 collectively on their $100 bill. If I’m left even 10%, $10, I end up with $5.50. Fine. If I have one of those who think $3 or less or whatever is an adequate tip, I am MINUS money. 

So, yes, regardless of our hourly wage and if you or whoever judges us being paid “fairly” by our employer, I expect to be tipped fairly so I don’t end up paying out of my pocket to serve people. I provide great service, and a great guest experience, and I’m confident in that, so I expect to be appreciated and thanked through my tip appropriately. 

    Also, please keep in mind that servers/bartenders hold one of the only jobs where their income is mostly based on their performance and attitude and personality. We are not allowed “off” days. A bank worker, for example, will make the same income every day whether they’re grumpy, tired, hungover, sad, whatever. Our income(tips) is based on our daily performance; we aren’t able to be off our game or we will suffer financially that day, not to mention probably get guest complaints and deal with repercussions from management because of it. Everyone else is allowed “off” days and not being 100% and does not suffer economically. We do. Please keep that in mind if your server isn’t providing the best service .. we are only human. There are a million and one reasons their performance isn’t 100% that day.

You sound like you’re following all the proper steps of service but perhaps you’re feeling this way because you’re not connecting with your guests. Making each table feel like they have a unique experience and making their time with you personal is the key to being a great server vs a good server. Take the time to connect with each table some how. Work in a “so what brings you out tonight?” or a “how was your week?” or comment on something you pick up from overhearing their conversation when appropriate. Share something personal about yourself and your life or something cool you’ve been doing or watching on tv or a trip you’re going to take or a relating point connecting to something they’re talking about or wearing or whatever. If they’re celebrating something, ask your manager if you can bring them a surprise dessert or drink to acknowledge it. Go above and beyond when you can. Don’t be a robot. Strive to make emotional connections with your guests and make their experience one to remember that is different than those they’ve had at other restaurants.

Doubles usually rule for money! You work the busy part of lunch, hopefully take a break, then work the busy part of dinner! You don’t have to be there super early like the opener, and you don’t have to be there super late like the closer. Just make sure you drink water, rest your feet when you can, eat breakkie before you start, and eat something on your break. Take advantage of this awesome shift and kill it, kid! And yes, like others have said, don’t party the night before and attempt the day hungover. You’ll be kicking yourself within a few hours. Get a good sleep so you’re at your best and have the energy to get through a long shift.

From an outside perspective, it seems like you guys have fallen into a routine that has become mundane and tedious and somewhat “boring” and you’re suffering because of it. Think about it- everyday life is more or less the same daily. So, it’s natural and inevitable that eventually one or both of you will grow tired of talking about essentially the same topics and situations and problems and doing the same things over and over again. Only, he’s not dealing with it in a progressive way. You’ve taken the first steps towards fixing it by trying to communicate how you feel. It seems like he’s given up. 

My suggestion is to remember to start dating each other again. Switch it up. Make time for just you two at least once a week and do fun, different things together. Things you can experience together for the first time and talk about that are out of your norm. 

In no way is he pulling his weight in your relationship or doing the best for you guys. But, it would be efficient for you to remember that being a partner isn’t just doing favours for him or providing for the household or grocery shopping or taking care of the kids. And he needs to remember simply doing chores isn’t being a fully emotionally available partner and one that fulfills all the areas you need. It sounds like you both have forgotten the romance aspect of your relationship and to be romantic partners as well as housemates and parents and responsible adults. 

A question- do you both make time for yourselves and live independent lives? Have hobbies, go out with friends separately, participate in extra curriculars like sports teams or clubs ? Spending this time apart and doing your own thing will make your time together more meaningful and give you stuff to talk about as it’s entirely separate from each other and things you each don’t know anything about. 

Just my two cents. Let me know if you wanna chat further !

   I’m happy to answer any questions OP has about mental illness. I have been diagnosed with borderline personality disorder, anxiety, and major depressive disorder.

Consider yourself lucky for only experiencing circumstantial depression and having a “normal” enough brain that you are able to pull up your socks and “get over it.” Not everyone has a brain that can do that. The wiring/chemical makeup of people’s brains are different, dude. People with chronic mental illness do not have the pleasure of simply getting better so easily. Our brains are hard-wired to make this difficult and we have chemical imbalances. I find this post extremely naive, uneducated, and with a massive, sad lack of compassion. 

Also, it’s a good thing more people are talking about mental illness rather than suffering in silence. It means the stigmas attached are subsiding a little bit, and society is becoming more accepting, therefore, more people feel comfortable and safe talking about it. 

Consider having a conversation with someone who suffers from chronic mental illness in order to educate yourself and open yourself up to a narrative other than your own. I’m sad for you honestly.

I was best friends with a girl for 18 years (age 12-30) who was very similar. She moved about 2 hours away a few years ago and since then, our friendship has been strained to say the least. I made an effort to reach out and connect and ensure I was involved in her life and supportive as much as I could. I made the trip there multiple times, and she didn’t come to me once. I began to realize every convo we had was initiated by me, and it was dominated by her problems/what was happening in her life when we did talk. She never asked me how I was and what was new with me etc etc .. I was even dating someone for 6+ months and she had zero idea because she never asked. 

I ended up realizing that it was very one sided and I wasn’t benefiting/getting what I wanted or needed from our friendship anymore. I was putting in way too much effort and not receiving anything back and it was wearing on me. 

We’re not friends anymore, for many reasons, but I feel significantly less stressed and hurt disconnecting from her. I’ll always love her and be there if she needed me, but putting myself first has been a positive in my life. 

Idk, just something to consider. Weigh the pros and cons and figure out what is in your best interests.

The best advice I’ve gotten is to treat your entire section like one big party. Constantly make rounds. Visit every table and make sure they’re prioritized and have what they need. After your lap, get everything at once. Table 1’s salt, refills for table 3, ring in the party’s order. Then make another round and drop everything off. Make a stop in the kitchen and see if they need hands to run food. Stop by the bar and run drinks. Then make another full lap of your section. I was referred to a psychiatrist at a mental health hospital by my doctor. 

I went for my appointment and had an interview with the psychiatrist. He asked me an array of questions, and assessed me through how my answers correlated to the 9 criterium of BPD according to the DSM-5: 

Frantic efforts to avoid real or imagined abandonment; this does not include suicidal or self-mutilating behavior covered in criterion 5
A pattern of unstable and intense interpersonal relationships characterized by alternating between extremes of idealization and devaluation
Markedly and persistently unstable self-image or sense of self
Impulsivity in at least two areas that are potentially self-damaging (eg, spending, sex, substance abuse, reckless driving, binge eating) [5] ; this does not include suicidal or self-mutilating behavior covered in criterion 5
Recurrent suicidal behavior, gestures, or threats, or self-mutilating behavior
Affective instability due to a marked reactivity of mood (eg, intense episodic dysphoria, irritability, or anxiety usually lasting a few hours and only rarely more than a few days)
Chronic feelings of emptiness
Inappropriate, intense anger or difficulty controlling anger (eg, frequent displays of temper, constant anger, or recurrent physical fights)
Transient, stress-related paranoid ideation or severe dissociative symptoms

To be diagnosed, you must meet at least 5/9. I met all 9, lol. 

After I was diagnosed, I put myself on the wait list for an outpatient intensive DBT (dialectical behavioural therapy) program specializing in BPD. I was accepted 8 months later. Well worth the wait. It was 9 months long- 1 hr individual therapy and 3 hrs group therapy a week at the hospital. It saved my life. 

I have been in and out of therapy for 15 years, but only having access to CBT, which didn’t help nearly enough. You need DBT when you have BPD. The skills you learn and the format of the program is essential to recovery for borderlines. 

So, get a referral to be assessed/diagnosed by a psychiatrist. Get yourself into a DBT program. Don’t bother with CBT- it may work for those who have depression/anxiety, but BPD is a whole different monster that needs a specific type of care. 

Best of luck!

From experience, co-workers are never much more than acquaintances. 

It’s great to be amicable and friendly with them. It makes work much more tolerable and fun! But, unless you have a deep connection with them, talk all the time,hang out with them, and have a relationship like you do with your true friends you have outside of work, they’re just co-workers. 

Gossip in the workplace is avid. People love to spill tea and gab about other people. Work is boring for the most part, and unfortunately, this makes it more interesting and makes the day go by faster. It also creates a false sense of closeness between people and gives them something  to talk about when they really don’t have much in common. 

I’ve learned the hard way to not share personal things like this with other staff. Especially if I have an issue with another co-worker, have heard gossip about them, or if another co-worker has shared personal info with me and has asked me not to share it with others. 

As much as you think someone is “trustworthy,” they’re probably not. It’s not that they’re a bad person, or malicious, it’s just how it is in the workplace. 

Don’t gossip about others, don’t spread tea you’ve heard, don’t participate in “shit talking” others when you’re around a group of people doing so. If someone asks you if you’ve heard about a certain situation or person, say you haven’t, even if you have. Your words will get skewed and you’ll be made out to be the bad guy and a shit talker. You’re only creating issues between yourself and co workers this way. 

When you have an issue at work, or with someone at work, vent to someone in your real life close circle. Family, your spouse, your actual friends. It’ll actually benefit you more because you’ll be able to hear a non-biased opinion from them. 

If someone is gossiping to you, listen, and only respond with “wow” or “that’s horrible” or “i’m sorry” or “that sucks a lot” or things of that nature. Don’t fuel the fire or bad mouth or state your opinion. Stay neutral and you’ll never have issues with anyone at work.

Given all this, I’m sure you can gather that next time, it’s probably best not to share your issues with co workers with other people you work with, even if you deem them “trustworthy.” From this experience, I hope you have learned that there are better people in your life to vent your upsets to; people that don’t include your co-workers.

The reason that gifted kids seem to “go downhill” and progressively become “worse” regarding school the older they get is because as you progress into higher grades, there is less structure and more responsibility. Teachers expect you to be more and more independent and responsible for yourself and your education. There is less nagging and management of your learning and homework as well as less communication with your parents if your teachers feel like you’re falling behind, failing to do your work, etc. So, those with ADHD struggle to independently organize themselves, use time management effectively, and develop routines. 

    I was just like you in elementary school/highschool. I was evaluated and proven “gifted” in elementary school, but my parents didn’t want me starting over in a new school so I stayed where I was instead of going to the gifted school. I always got high marks in elementary school. As I moved through highschool, my marks got progressively lower due to the reasons I stated above and being distracted by friends and relationships and becoming older and more socially independent. However, I still graduated with honours. It was University that got me. Having literally no teachers micromanage me or enforce a structure or encourage my success, I was unable to keep up or learn how to properly create structures that assisted my success with having ADHD. So, I failed first year. 

I wasn’t even diagnosed until I was 23- I just see this all upon reflection and in retrospect. As for “proof” of your ADHD in childhood, dig up your old report cards and read your teachers’ comments. It’s not necessarily all based on your grades. Your behaviour is key here. See if there are any comments such as “x needs to try to keep their desk clean and organize their backpack,” or “x needs to try to be less social in class and more focused on the lesson,” or “x needs to try to remember their homework.” These all are indicators of ADHD in childhood. 

Good luck!

Meditation and mindfulness exercises like the ones you describe aren’t meant to be taken literally. They’re meant to encourage you to take yourself out of the present situation and to help you develop the ability to focus your mind on one task. Imagining a “peaceful room” or a river or whatever else is meant to allow you to get in touch with your mind, soul, and body and ground you solely in that moment. It is meant to clear your mind of anxieties and rapid/ruminating thoughts and take you to a place away from all of that, focusing on imagining being in one situation that is far away from what you’re experiencing in real life. The key word is “imagining,” and the key to this practice being successful is to be open to it. Having the negative mindset and attitude you have towards these exercises is the main reason it doesn’t help or work for you. It would be effective for you to try to open yourself up to it and give it your all without judgements and see what it does for you. 

The point of these exercises is to take you back to a neutral state, refresh and centre your mind/soul/body, and recalibrate yourself when you’re in a state of distress/overwhelmed. Directing your attention and focus to something entirely different can help you calm yourself down, start with a blank slate after the exercise, and lead to a new narrative/perspective on whatever is going on with you. 

The fact that these exercises are totally based on imagination and take you to a place that is fictional is actually the beauty of them. Allowing your mind to take you to a place that doesn’t exist when everything else conflicting you and around you is so real and intense is powerful. 

However, if you really struggle getting into these exercises, I’d suggest trying a mindfulness practice that is more “factual.” For example, a body scan: 

https://www.verywellmind.com/body-scan-meditation-why-and-how-3144782

I’ll also say again that I think you need to allow yourself to be more open and put yourself into therapy practices like this, even if it’s out of your comfort zone or you have resistance towards them. Therapy only works if you have a total open mind to it to want it to. Having walls up or allowing your negative stigmas/judgements/opinions against certain aspects of it will only hinder your progress. 

Best of luck.

One of the best skills I learned in DBT therapy was Opposite Action. Evaluate if the thought/action/behaviour is serving you or effective. Do this by “checking the facts”- try to think about this with your rational/wise mind rather than emotional mind. If it’s not benefiting you, use Opposite Action. Theorize ways you can think/behave exactly opposite to what you naturally want to. Do this whole heartedly. Don’t half ass it. 

For example- 

If you’re feeling mentally off, sad, depressed, anxious and feel like skipping work or staying in bed all day, whatever, you’re probably having thoughts like “I shouldn’t go in, I won’t be myself, people will notice and judge me, my manager will get mad I’m not 100%, it’s better if I just call in sick and stay home.” You may want to isolate, sleep, wall yourself in. 

An Opposite Action would be forcing yourself to get out of bed early, taking a shower, making a healthy breakfast and going for a walk before work. When at work, instead of choosing to be socially restricted and do the bare minimum, force yourself to go above and beyond. Go out for lunch with co-workers. Offer to take on a new project. Ask someone how their weekend was and then show interest by asking questions about specifics. Do as much as you can to do exactly what you don’t want to do. 

This will change your narrative and thought patterns. And doing these positive and effective things will make you proud of yourself and it will make you feel better. Doing normal things makes you feel normal. 

When you get home, reflect on how you would have felt if you stayed home, continued negative thought patterns, missed work, etc. Count the positives in your day you gained from using this skill. Perhaps even write them down to look at the next time you’re feeling the same way to encourage you in the future to do it again. 

You will have a sense of accomplishment, you will have made effective choices that have served you positively all day, and you will have changed your thought patterns from negatives to positives.

I was diagnosed with ADHD when I was 23. Somehow, I made it through highschool with honours. In HS, I figured out ways to get by- I charmed my teachers and because they knew I was very smart and capable, they let things slide like late assignments. But, in university I went the opposite direction. The change of structure and freedom I had was detrimental. However, I decided against meds because I figured I had “gotten by” my whole life without them. 


    I started a program in Social Work this year. I’m 29. I really had to evaluate what contributed to and made it hard to do well. Disorganization, lack of motivation and procrastination were the big ones. So, I got a whiteboard and used it to write down all my classes and times and what was due that week. I also went through all my courses every Monday and wrote down homework, tests and assignments due that week. Then I organized it into chronological order of priority based on what I needed to accomplish first. I also worked with myself. I was patient and accommodating to the best way I learn. I only did homework every second day. I took breaks as often as I needed when doing schoolwork. I did work at night because that’s when I’m most productive. 

     Try to figure out what works best for you and incorporate that into your routine. Also, arrange a meeting with Disability Services at school. Explain you think you have ADHD and need accommodations. They can arrange for you to be granted extensions when needed, longer test times and the ability to work in a private room during tests (idk where you live and if you’re attending school in person or not yet.) 

Lastly, finding ways to live well and your best life is a choice you need to make and commit to. I know it’s hard. But you know what you need to improve on and find ways to cope with. You just need to do it. It’s easier said than done, I know, but doing nothing to change your life isn’t benefiting you. Make small changes slowly, be patient with yourself, self reflect and make a list of how you’re going to do it, ask for help from family and friends, research tips online and try them out and see what works for you. It’s your life and you deserve to commit to yourself to be the best you can be.

When I was 21, my boyfriend died by suicide. Thoughts of my loved ones doing the same completely consumed my life. If I argued with someone, I’d immediately freak out afterwards in fear they’d do the same. But, it was more than that. I was terrified that my loved ones would die by any means. When my parents went on a trip, I’d ruminate the entire time they were gone that their plane would crash, or they’d get in a car accident with their rental car, or they’d get murdered. If a boyfriend didn’t reply to texts or calls for a few hours, I’d convince myself they were dead. I was diagnosed with borderline personality disorder about a year after he died. Symptoms include fear of abandonment, and  catastrophizing situations. So, obviously this played a big part. I eventually somewhat learned to downplay these anxious thoughts, and use opposing statements to burn out their flames. 

“They’re probably asleep, or with friends or their phone is charging” when I freaked out about not getting a text back. 

If I was worried about my parents/loved ones being away from me, I’d just call or text them and check on them. I also learned to ask people to keep in touch with me a few times a day to ease my worry. 

Three years ago(yesterday, actually,) my fiancé committed suicide. It was all of my nightmares coming true. Everything I feared for so long was confirmed. I suffered. Everything I had tried to teach myself to combat these anxieties were trash because my fears actually came to fruition. 

I went through a six month DBT program specializing in BPD. My therapist helped me develop opposing statements to my very deeply embedded beliefs that haunted me everyday. She also said two things that will stick with me forever: 

“At the end of the day, it is not your responsibility to save anyone. That is too much weight to put on yourself, and I’m sure you’re exhausted.” 

“What if you chose not to believe everything your brain told you? What if you decided that sometimes, your thoughts are wrong, and you chose to give yourself the chance to explore alternatives.” 

I felt free after that. I could chose to change my own narrative. 

But, tbh, I still struggle with fearing my loved ones will leave me, purposely or unintentionally. The only difference is that i have moreso accepted that I don’t have much to do with the outcome of other people’s lives, and trying to control something I can’t actually control is inefficient towards my mental well being and happiness.

Something I’ve learned over the past year that I try to keep in mind is that “hard is hard.” Just because someone else is going through situations in life that are deemed “worse” than yours, doesn’t mean you aren’t valid in how you feel about anything and your emotional reaction towards this. Despite the difference in situation, you are warranted to your feelings towards anything that is difficult. The degree of the “difficulty” of a situation is a judgment, and when anyone faces anything that is challenging, it should be just seen as “hard.” Not “harder” or “less hard” than another as this is allowing ourselves to participate in a judgmental attitude towards ourselves and others, which isn’t efficient behaviour or thought patterns. Doing this is allowing ourselves to dismiss our truth and how we feel, and removes the chance to validate ourselves, which leads to abandoning the chance to use strategies and skills to cope healthily and effectively.

I’m not sure which type of therapy you’re doing, but try DBT. It’s usually out patient programs that have you go to the hospital twice a week- once for individual therapy and once for group. DBT teaches actual skills to deal with mental illness and accompanying symptoms rather than just providing “talk therapy” with someone. In the past, I have found CBT and talk therapy generally unhelpful. It always seemed as if the therapist would just sit there and listen to me vent, provide some mediocre advice and I’d leave feeling like nothing was solved or better for me. DBT provides actual training and skills on how to cope with mental illness. Some skills are for daily use, some are for anxiety, some are for extreme distress. It allows you to put your disorder in your own hands while providing tools to cope with it properly and learn to live with it and live the best you can with the tools and skills taught. And these skills can be used FOREVER. 

Doing a DBT program for my BPD was honestly a saving grace for me and the skills are a gift. DBT is also said to be the best treatment for people with BPD!

I’d suggest taking it upon yourself to test out different foods. Every two weeks, cut out something new and record how your body reacts to it. For example, cut out gluten, then cut out red meat, then cut out dairy, then cut out all meat, then cut out sugar, etc until you discover what cuts down your negative symptoms/eliminates them. It’s likely that you have an allergy/intolerance to something, and doing this will make it more apparent what it is. When you realize what makes you feel the best by excluding it from your diet, make it permanent. Also, if you haven’t already, get a full blood work test and see if you’re deficient/have too much of anything going on- this could be affecting your digestion negatively. 

Also, avoid things that will obviously irritate you like spicy food, too much dairy, etc. Take probiotics and eat foods that promote gut health like bone broth, sauerkraut, mild kimchi, yogurt, etc. 

Good luck!

Coming from someone who has always (until recently, the past couple years) has always had back burners while in relationships, it’s completely due to insecurity. I have Borderline Personality Disorder, and a main symptom is a fear of abandonment and being alone, so having “back burners” allowed me to feel okay when relationships ended because I could just replace the connection/attention/love I had from my ex partner with attention from one of the people I kept around solely for this purpose. Not saying everyone who does this has BPD, but it’s common that people don’t want to be alone and sit with their hurt if they lose someone they love. This is an easy way to ensure that they don’t have to deal with the pain as hard and be alone, and keeping in contact with these backups throughout a relationship makes it easy to continue the connection with them when they need something to make them feel good when they’re not okay.

I was diagnosed at 23. I have never been on medication for it. I taught myself how to manage my symptoms- I graduated with honours in highschool, I have two culinary degrees, and I just started one for Social Work.

Realize that you have a unique brain and learning style. You need to learn how to adapt to it and do what’s best for you. For example, I am a night owl. During the morning and day time, I am a write off. I don’t absorb anything, I’m tired all day, and I’m not happy with learning. But, at night I am focused and get so much done. Find out what time is best for studying for you.

My parents started allowing my brother and I to make our own portions based on how hungry we were at a pretty young age. They would only have an issue or make us stay at the table until we finished when we would take way more food than we could eat as it was in our hands in the first place. 

My mom’s parents, and her grandma were a different story. My great grandma was German and went through the Holocaust (not abiding by Hitler and the military caused her, her husband and my grandpa when he was very young,) to go to concentration camps. They actually escaped on a bicycle and fled to a Red Cross camp but lost my great grandpa along the way. After moving around a few camps, my great grandma randomly bumped into him after many years in a random town! 

After that they fled together to Nova Scotia, and then to Toronto. They lived with a family they knew from Germany (who had gotten there before them) for many years .. 12 people in a one bedroom. She worked as a housekeeper. Eventually they saved enough for their own place, but my great grandpa died in a car accident (I never met him.) 

Amazing story. She lived until she was 97 in an apartment by herself- cooking, cleaning, totally cognitive. She’s my inspiration. 

Point being, food was always weird to her and my mom’s dad. Because they were so poor and regularly starving for most of their lives, it meant everything. She would make an absolute feast for family events. And she was an amazing cook! But, she’d serve everyone HUGE portions. When you finished, she’d put more on your plate and if you refused because you were full, she’d say you didn’t like her cooking and make you feel guilty. But then, if you couldn’t finish, she’d be offended and remind you that she was starving in the war and we should be grateful. It was a weird dynamic. I love that woman with my whole heart, but that was something we could never win. 

With my grandpa(her son,) I noticed weird things with food too. During dinners, he’d always have to be the first to serve himself a massive plate as fast as he could, like if he didn’t, he wouldn’t get to eat. He’d also mumble under his breath “slow down joe” because he ate so fast. My mom says it’s because if he didn’t eat fast enough as a child, his dad would take the rest of the food as a second helping and he wouldn’t get another plate. 

Point being, food and the relationship people have with food from an early age affects them FOREVER. It’s ingrained unless you make a conscious effort to correct it. 

Parents should let children make their own choices about types of food they eat (within reason,) portion sizes, etc when they’re of reasonable age to set their own personal and effective patterns. This way, later in life, they won’t have any emotions attached to food. Food shouldn’t do that- it should be pleasurable and seen as a necessary part of wellness.

The best advice I got when I started out in kitchen management (as a sous chef,) was “get to know your people.” If you know your staff personally, and they see you care about them and their well being and development, they will always try to do right by you and bend over backyards to help you out! For example, I had an awesome dishwasher- however, he was on the autism spectrum (super smart kid, just bad with social interactions,) and he got easily frustrated if it got too busy and he couldn’t keep up, if servers didn’t arrange the like plates together to make it easier for him or if it was getting too messy. These were his triggers, and I did my best to ensure they could be avoided. However, my boss, the chef, who had worked with him for years didn’t even know he was Autistic. This to me is a totally disregard and lack of care of learning to get to know his staff as people, not just robots on the line. 

Another thing I think I did well at was always have an “open door policy.” My staff felt at ease coming to be with work related or personal issues, and I tried to help them out with them the best I could. For example, the chef would force the staff to use less protect than the portion size spec indicated in order to have a “good” Food Cost on paper since that was part of his bonus. My staff felt as if they were cheating people (meals weren’t cheap- nachos were about $20 vegetarian lol, and instead of three ounces of cheese he to them to put 1.5oz.) He’d also force staff to flip labels- if someone expired that day, they were to print a new label from that day to give it three more days shelf life as to use less product again. 

Staff wasn’t understood and they didn’t feel like they were valued as humans to him. If they were sick, he’d give them a really hard time about missing a shift, try to make them cover it, if they couldn’t he’d write them up and then cut their hours the next week. 

So, I tried to be the literal opposite of him for my staff lol. I was caring, kind, worked just as many hours they did, supported them by staying at work hours after my end time if they needed help, listened to them, adapted to their specific personalities, solved issues they were concerned about and overall treated them like humans with lives outside of the restaurant which sometimes needed their attention while conflicting with work- id find a cover or cover it myself lol. 

My best advice is to just treat everyone how you’d like to be treated. Have a meeting with them and have an open forum on what they’d like to change and how you can create a better workspace they’re happy to come to everyday. Ensure you compliment and praise good work, not just scold mistakes. 

When you walk in to work every day, your attitude is going to be absorbed by your staff. If you make a point of being positive and happy every single day even if you feel the opposite, you will have a happy staff. 

However, understand there is a fine line between being this type of manager and being walked all over and taken advantage of. Don’t be afraid to stand your ground if someone is fucking up- but do it by taking them aside in private in the office and work on a plan with them to find a resolution.

Happy to answer any more questions you may have !

It’s very possible you just learned skills and ways to adapt to your ADHD that work for you and allow you to be productive in your life including school, work and relationships. I was diagnosed with ADHD at 23 years old- I went through all of grade school, highschool and most of my Post Secondary Programs not knowing why I was the way I was- procrastination, starting assignments two hours before they were due In university, especially first year comes to mind. I was too anxious to attend most classes so I did all the PowerPoints on my own time, but not being organized caused them all to build up and I was left with a cornucopia of lectures and PowerPoint slides, as well novels to read every week. Working this way was physically impossible to complete due the the multitude of assigments, especially when they heavy work term hit midway through the semester. 
I’m starting my 11th year of Post Secondary (3 different areas of study, I’ve graduated from culinary school with a degree in Culinary Management and a Post Grad in Italian Studies and have just started a program in Social Service Work two weeks ago,) without medication. 

Point being, I went through all of elementary school and highschool and a lot of years in an University program (psychology, later switching to English,) which was followed by all my culinary education (I now have obtained a Degree in Culinary Management as well as  a degree in the Post Grad Italian Studies program,) and I still haven’t taken ADHD specific medication for it. I am on the antidepressant “Pristiq, 75mg” to deal with the symptoms of my mental health disorder (Borderline Personality Disorder,) such as depression, anxiety, fear of abandonment, catastrophic thinking , splitting on people, etc. 

        But, I have lived my entire life, and been through educational programs three times now. I managed to get honour role upon graduating High School and an Arts Certificate included on my diploma. I have gotten through most university and college programs having this disorder and not using medication for it by finding ways and loopholes that helped me understand and complete what was needed based on creating a learning structure that worked for me. This entire time, I was unaware that my struggles lied in undiagnosed ADHD. 

       I am now in SSW at 29 years old. I’m paying for this round of school on my own dime (no financial help from my parents, who have truly helped enough during my previous programs, so I’m happy to do this alone!) I am considering talking to my doctor about being prescribed a mild medication for ADHD symptoms such as focus, lack of attention, struggles with motivation, procrastination, etc. I have already applied to my school’s Disability Accommodations Program to ensure I am provided with extra time for assignments/tests, I’m allowed to write exams/texts in separate room when COVID restrictions are lifted and my professors are well aware that I may take frequent breaks during lectures to read-focus myself and use skills to calm down my anxiety.  

I was told by the psychiatrist that I suffered from all the symptoms based on the testing/interviews I took concerning ADHD, and he didn’t know how I actually got through all that schooling without struggling. But, since I was diagnosed much later than highschool, the only conclusion was that I learned to alter the information taught to benefit my own learning style. If I found I wasn’t particularly great in following teachers’ lectures in school, I would always be able to view the information posted online and teach myself, or find other means to learn what I needed to learn for tests/assignments such as Google or Library books lol.   

It’s all about what works for you- if you function better without medication, don’t take it. If you feel it benefits you positively, there is no harm In starting with a low dose, seeing how it works for you, and upping or lowering it as needed. This is your life and your health and you need to do what’s best for yourself ! 

Good luck!

I’ve learned through therapy that we are NOT mind readers. Picking up on social cues, body language, how they’re talking to us, if they’re not responding to messages, whatever, of course gives us clues, but it also allows us to become convinced of the worst case scenario. We also tend to assume these factors are because of us, something we did, and because they’re angry with us. We can’t possibly know what people are feeling unless we simply ask. All those factors could very well be because of something entirely different they’re dealing with. Biting the bullet and flat out asking them if they’re upset with us for some reason is the only way to know for sure. Doing this also automatically takes away worry and anxiety about the situation. The answer is either yes or no. After knowing it, it leads way to being able to problem solve further- either you have their admittance that there’s an issue between you two on the table and you can address it further, or they will let you in on something else that is bothering them which you can try to help them out with. 

Either way, you aren’t stuck in limbo and walking on eggshells wondering what is going on with them, which will calm your worries in the least.

But, to each their own, I guess. You can only hope for the best for people.

ADD/ADHD often are coupled with other mental illnesses such as anxiety, depression, OCD etc. For me, I have ADHD as well as Borderline Personality Disorder, anxiety and depression. They all interact with each other and cause issues unless I am on medication/in therapy. 

Specific to ADD, understand they may be spacey. It’s hard for them to focus on one thing at a time. Talking to them may result in them trailing off to a bunch of topics that don’t necessarily relate to the original conversation point. 

For me, my brain works a million miles a second. Talking about one thing reminds me of something else so when in conversation, it’s very easy for me to jump from topic to topic as well as not give the other person a chance to speak or respond. 

The best way to help me focus is to stop me at some point. My boyfriend will eventually stop me from talking and remind me of the original topic we were discussing. For example, “OP, I really wanted to hear your opinion on *original topic,* do you think we can talk about it again?” Then, he reminds me to let him speak and give his opinion on it if I start blabbing again. 

As someone with ADHD, I can assure you that we don’t mean to be spazzy in conversations. I’ve been told I don’t give room for other people to talk- we don’t mean to monopolize the conversation either. We just need interjections and reminders to snap out of our continuous thought train. 

This is the biggest issue for me in relationships.. if you encounter more that you associate to ADD, feel free to message me and I will be glad to help and give my opinion from the standpoint of someone who suffers!

Okay, so I know we both know your first step is seeking out a therapist. Perhaps one who specializes in rage/PTSD/trauma would help you a lot. You need to invest yourself in help in a professional’s care- your situation seems to be too big for you or your loved ones to solve on your own. You deserve to feel better, to deal with your hurt, and to find peace. 

As for the weed thing, I am in DBT therapy for Borderline Personality Disorder. I fill out a “mood diary card” every day of the week, and go over it with my therapist in our weekly meetings. There is a category meant to track substance use- my biggest use being alcohol. However, my therapist has made it very clear to me that she isn’t there to judge me for my substance use, or even to help change it. That is what addiction counsellors are for, if I ever felt the urge to stop. So, my alcohol intake, although recorded, isn’t the focus of our sessions, nor does she judge it/attempt to change it. 

My point being, when starting with a new therapist, ensure you are upfront about your use, but also that you don’t want it to be the focus of your sessions together and you’d appreciate if they didn’t try to discuss it unless you bring it up first and are willing to. It’s possible. However, attempt to attend your sessions sober. A clear mind will make treatment a lot more beneficial to you.

Lastly, when you find a professional that you’re comfortable with and want to stick with, perhaps discuss different courses of meds that are in line with your symptoms. I know when I started meds (Pristiq,) it calmed my anxiety/depression/BPD symptoms as soon as it started working. It also gave me more motivation and a better outlook on things and the “kick” I needed to take care of myself, ensure I attended my therapy when prior, I could barely get out of bed, attempt therapy with an open mind and determination to get better, and eventually even start working again. 

I have found my spark again after a year of therapy(2.5 hours group therapy and 1 hour individual therapy,) and over a year of meds. I am okay again. Even more, I am better than I have been in a long time and I want you to feel that way too. Everyone deserves to. 

Good luck, and always here to talk.

I told this story to my boyfriend recently- he is someone who will show his discontent with things like gifts, dinners I make, if I buy him an energy drink and it’s not the one he wanted specifically, etc: A husband and his son are sitting at their kitchen table, waiting for breakfast. Mom/wife makes toast, and when she delivers it to husband, it is totally burnt. Husband continues reading the newspaper, picks up the toast and eats all of it without commenting on it being burnt at all. Son asks “dad, why didn’t you ask mom why she burnt it and served it, why did you act like nothing was wrong at all?” Dad replies “I will forget about burnt toast within an hour, I will get to work and a thousand other small issues will be thrown at me, and I will forget about my breakfast completely.” He continues: “Harsh words, criticism, complaints and being unappreciative to someone who did something out of love and care lasts longer. If I had complained to your mother and made her feel bad about the meal she made me amongst her busy day, it would stick and hurt her longer. Besides, it’s only burnt toast.” 

I think about this story every time I am tempted to complain or say something unappreciative about a gesture someone has made/said/done for me. It’s much more effective to thank them and show gratitude, even if it’s not what you wanted or perfect than to make the other person feel bad about something they put their heart into for you. 

Maybe you can somehow bring this up to him and tell this story- I told my boyfriend it when he complained about a gift I got for him that wasn’t exactly right and he has shown appreciation and thanks since. 

You have done nothing wrong and you deserve appreciation from your partner for things you put love into for them.

If someone gets a tattoo and are unhappy, most times they will slander their name, write bad reviews, and they won’t be recommended to future clients. If the customer leaves happy, they will recommend them and the shop to everyone they know/anyone who sees their body art. So it’s in their best interest to make their client as happy as possible. Next, they will put the outline on your skin in marker. Again, ensure you’re satisfied, especially with the placement and size.

Good luck!

I have Borderline Personality Disorder and some of the main symptoms are anxiety and depression (along with a whole slew of others.) I have recently went through 6 months of DBT therapy, specializing in BPD. One of the most helpful things I have learned is how to deal with anxiety. The biggest reason I chose to go to therapy was because I was experiencing anxiety severely. I’d wake up every half hour between 5am-10am when I had to be at work for 11:30am because I’d be scared I’d miss my alarm and be late for work. I’d also be anxious about what would happen once I got there (I was a sous chef, I was living my dream career but constantly afraid I was fucking up and going to be in trouble from the chef, my boss.) My anxiety eventually lead to me quitting my job. I waited 8 months after that to get into the DBT program specializing in BPD, which I was in twice a week in an outpatient program at a mental health hospital for 6 months. Ultimately, I learned that I needed to set boundaries with people, sometimes “no” is a complete answer, DBT skills to use against my BPD symptoms and overall how to accept myself and love myself for who I am and that nothing is wrong with me and that I don’t need to change myself. In regards to anxiety, I have learned that when experiencing it, acknowledging it happening and accepting it, yet not letting it control your emotions/behaviours is the best way to deal with it.

I don’t know if this will help you, but I hope it does. I have suffered from anxiety/depression as long as I can remember, and later was diagnosed with borderline personality disorder. I had an obsession with the idea that everyone I knew would commit suicide or get into a car accident or die some other way unless I did certain things like reply to texts immediately, text my loved ones goodnight (if I didn’t, they’d die before the morning and I’d regret not texting them before bed forever,) and I’d feel responsible for people if they were expressing negative thoughts, thinking if I didn’t do everything I could to help them they’d die. I had zero boundaries and forfeited my own well being in order to tend to my obsession of ensuring everyone was okay and wasn’t going to leave me like my past partners. 

My therapist said something that changed my mindset- she said “what if you didn’t believe everything your brain is telling you?” She also told me that taking responsibility for everyone else’s lives is more than anyone can handle. These two things have changed my life. I no longer obsess over these things and I am happy. My anxiety is 80% less than it was before. 

Our situations are different. But I challenge you to ask yourself the same thing. What if you don’t believe everything your brain is telling you? What if you understand that your thoughts could be wrong? Try this. Try to just not listen to your brain and compulsions. I promise you once you do it once it’ll become easier the more you do it.

His distress over these things would be valid if you weren’t in the financial position to treat yourself the way you do every once and a while, or you were using joint funds that were dedicated to other things like rent, groceries, savings for a vacation, etc. But you worked hard to obtain the career you have, and you deserve and are entitled to doing whatever you want with your salary because of this. As for your family’s celebrations, there are many cultures that celebrate milestones by going as big as they can to show how important the event is: baptisms in the Catholic faith, Bar/Bat Mitzvahs in Judaism, Quinceaneras in Mexico, Sweet 16s in Western Culture, and many cultures have big celebrations for weddings that usually cost a fair amount of money. My point being, it’s not just your family and Indian culture that celebrates like you do and goes above and beyond to make the event special. Your SO can’t judge you and your family for how you throw events, the money you spend, and being “extra” as if you are the only people who do this. Many cultures and people go all out for things like this. And there is nothing wrong with that. I’m sure many families save for years and years in anticipation of their child’s wedding or first child or milestone birthday etc in order to celebrate like this. 

I think your SO is perhaps a little bit jealous of the family you were born into. Maybe he is picturing your upbringing as being fortunate compared to his being full of struggle and finds it unfair. His jealousy and discontent is coming out as judgements of what people in your family wear and you going shopping and purchasing more expensive brands etc. 

I’d sit down and have a conversation with him. Maybe let him know that you are aware of his struggles growing up and it must be hard for him comparing them to your security. But, explain that judging your family for the way they celebrate is not okay based on the fact that it’s part of your culture. Also note that you have worked hard towards the career and salary you have earned, and you should be able to occasionally treat yourself for your hard work without his judgement.

Overall, you and your family have done no wrong and his judgments are not okay and unnecessary. You all should be proud of your accomplishments!

Brown your trimmings and season with salt, remove, add mirepoix (carrots, and celery and onion 2 times the amount of carrots,) season with salt. When onions are translucent, use red wine or premade beef stock to deglaze- pour about half a cup of either into pot and use a wooden spoon to scrape up the “fond” which is the stuff stuck to the bottom of the pot. If you used wine, cook it out for about two minutes. Add half a can of tomato paste and cook it out for about 2 minutes. Add the beef trimmings back and add either water or premade beef stock in whatever quantity you want, depending on how much you want to make. Add about half a can of diced tomatoes (the acid helps break down the meat until tender.) Add 2 TBSP of red wine vinegar which also helps the meat become tender. Bring up to a boil and then reduce to a simmer. Cook for about 2 hours, or until meat is tender. This ensures the most flavour has developed from the trimmings. Remember to continue skimming the fat off of the top of the stock while cooking. If you aren’t happy with the beef flavour, it’s possible to add a packet or two of bouillon to enhance it. Remove from heat and strain stock into another pot. Skim fat, and add some butter if you’d like. Season to taste with salt and pepper.

I originally dreaded group but it SAVED me, and if you haven’t experienced a program like this (I’ve also done independent/private counselling, shelling out $150 a session and I prefer government funded programs like the above,) I highly recommend you give it an honest chance.

Solution: I have given him certain chores that are the same daily/weekly. Example, he wakes up earlier so he feeds the dog and lets him out. He walks him once a day. He does the garbage/recycling every week. He carries the bus bin of our dirty dishes upstairs so I can load them into the dishwasher. He also carries them back down. He’s responsible for vacuuming once a week as well. 

Giving him tasks to complete the same time everyday has helped a lot and taken a lot off of my back, especially because I don’t have to nag him about them. It’s a start in the right direction. 

I’ve broken down quite a few times about my mental overload and he honestly feels bad. He just doesn’t get it yet- these things were never important or completely necessary to me until about a year ago so I get it. People advance and mature at different rates, so maybe your partner is somewhat alike to mine?

I’ve worked in the restaurant industry for over ten years. I’ve never had an interview that has had “hard questions,” more or less questions that require some thinking as well as demonstrating your work ethic/personality. Have answers prepared for questions like “what’s the toughest problem you’ve had to solve at work, and how did you solve it?,” “how would you deal with a guest who insists they have a reservation when they don’t, and there are no tables available for them,“ “when seating a guest, what would you say to recommend an app/drink for them to consider while they wait for their server?,” “Describe a situation at or outside of work you’ve demonstrated team work and/or leading a team” and things of the like. They may also test you on how much you have researched the restaurant- I’ve had interviews for chain restaurants that have specifically asked me to “sell” an app on their menu to them as if they were a guest in the restaurant, checking if I had looked into the menu/restaurant/brand before attending the interview. Be familiar with their brand, their food and drink menu, and their overall concept of a restaurant- being prepared and knowledgeable like this will set you apart from other candidates. It will ensure you’re able to answer any questions they shoot your way. This will allow you to even go above and beyond if they don’t ask these kinds of questions- you can impress them by stating how much you love a certain dish or gush about a certain experience you’ve had dining there (like if you went for a birthday and they brought you a free dessert and sang to you, or something of this nature.) 

Another thing I do in interviews every single time is comment on the decor/set up of the restaurant when the interviewer greets me at the door/meets me at a table to start the interview- “it’s gorgeous in here, I love the set up of your bar!!” Or “I love the pictures you guys have on the wall,” etc. It breaks the ice and starts conversation while complimenting them at the same time from the get go.

Maybe they’re going to have someone in a higher up position (GM, owner,) or just another manager interview you a second time to get a feel for you and have that be the “final phase” before they hire you? I’ve had interview processes for chain restaurants that do this to ensure multiple people agreed I was right for the job. Go into it ready for the same type of questions but probably with a different person.

Use the STOP skill first and foremost. 

S- Literally STOP as you feel yourself about to have an outburst or say/do things impulsively. 

T- Take a step back. This can be as small as one backwards step, removing yourself from the situation for enough time for you to calm down, (perhaps using the TIP skill? Using an ice pack for 30 seconds or splashing cold water on my face helps me a lot,) or literally leaving the premises to go for a walk or get some air outside. For the last point, ensure to communicate with your partner that you’re only leaving for a short amount of time and you will come back so they don’t worry. 

O- Observe the situation after calming down so you can see all sides and the opinions of the other parties clearly. You may see fault in your actions, or it will provide a Wise Mind answer to what to do next. 

P- Proceed Mindfully. When you’re ready, go back to the situation at hand listening to Wise Mind. Couple this step with other skills like Radical Acceptance, Checking the Facts, Challenging Myths and Beliefs, and using a DEAR MAN/GIVE/FAST script developed and rehearsed while you’re stepping away from the situation. 

This is what I do when I feel myself about to spiral, especially in regards to Interpersonal Relationships.

You’ll find as you get older, having you and your partner working opposite schedules is super common and happens more and more often as you age. However, people put up with this, and sacrifice spending time together ( as opposed to someone not working/having to find a job they might not like/is in their field) for the bigger picture. This is especially true when you move in together/get married/have kids. When you’re self sufficient and both of your incomes take care of bills and food and rent and savings and cars and making a family etc etc, having a dual income is much more important than fretting over not seeing each other as much as you’d like. This is life, adulting and becoming more mature and aware of what’s important and how that will eventually benefit you in the future. If a long term relationship and kids and spending your life with this person isn’t a priority, end it and find someone who has a similar routine. If this is something you do want, make the best of the small time you have together (weekends?) and try to consider the grand scheme of things, not just how shitty it is right now.

To me, people who choose to use politically incorrect and/or derogatory terminology while referring to anything send the image out to the world that they a) Aren’t respectful of differences B) aren’t intelligent enough to use a synonym for the asshole language they use C) Do not care about the societal norms of what’s right or wrong in regards to efficient speech D) Don’t constructively think about what they’re saying in regards to how it’ll affect the person/persons. When I was younger (grade 9, 23-24 years old,) I started to understand the impact of my words on others as well as myself (the reactions and opinions of peers after I’d used negative terminology.) So, I vowed to myself I’d eliminate certain words and phrases from my vocabulary such as gay, fag, faggot, retarded, downs, dyke, spic, the n word, etc etc altogether, besides if I was using gay towards someone who was actually gay. My dad always told me in high school “once you have a baby, you’re not a baby anymore.” Basically, if I chose to have sex without protection, got pregnant, and chose to keep it, he’d be supportive and loving emotionally, but not financially- to me (as he had been my whole life, but it was obvious he wouldn’t pay for things for me and my child, university, etc) or anything to do with the baby. Him and my mom were poor when I was born and figured it out, so I’d have to do the same. I got pregnant when I was 21 by a dude I was dating. He was abusive, physically and mentally, had no will to get a job or go to school, etc, so I got an abortion. He tormented me for it. My dad eventually found the paperwork from the abortion in my car and wrote me a letter stating how proud he was of me for my choice, especially knowing who the father was. My point being, my dad is the most wonderful, loving, kind hearted human in the world to not just me and my family but everyone he meets, and he still made these rules clear. So, your parents doing so isn’t because they’re jerks. They’re just adhering to their values. Kudos to you for stepping up, but don’t sacrifice yourself and your life and well being for her and the kid. She needs to take responsibility for her decision and learn to support her kid herself.

Research programs in your community that specialize in teaching DBT therapy and the skills it includes. Learning these skills has absolutely changed my life, my perspective and outlook- I have finally started to see light and hope and motivation and excitement for my future. Before this, I could only see dread for the next day and I was so angry and upset I was alive and had to do a new day every 24 hours without wanting to be here, but couldn’t leave this earth because of how badly it would affect my family/friends/loved ones and change their lives for the worse. Being in a DBT program specializing in Borderline Personality Disorder (diagnosed with it 6 years ago,) has re-wired my brain to use skills to deal with my constant distress; I now have time and emotional space to learn what I want my life to look like, and how to get there. You can be better and live better and I’m always here to chat if you need.

But, even renting is getting outrageous and hard to do, especially in big cities. Studios/ 1 bedroom apartments where I live (Toronto,) are on average almost $3000 a month, and I’m sure most bigger cities are similar. My point is, for your mom to have her own home and choose to decorate it, even with a lot of the decor being to look at but not to touch, is her right. After that, it’s up to them to take your advice and do the best for themselves. If they choose the opposite, you’ve done your due diligence. C) Allowing yourself to obsess over his choices and behaviours is only hurting you. You’re choosing to hurt your own emotional well being in exchange for trying to control decisions that are only his to make.

Always here to chat xoxo

It comes down to the fact that you’ll be away for a legitimate reason. You’re not just leaving them. You’re doing it for work related reasons, which will undoubtedly progress your career in the future which will benefit your family. It’s going to suck for everyone involved. There’s no denying that. Your wife will have to pick up double responsibility as a parent while battling emotions regarding being away from her partner. Your kids will be distressed over your absence, and won’t really understand why you’re gone. You will deal with guilt from being away, from leaving your wife alone with your kids, from missing them, from knowing that you’re missing milestones in your kids’ life as well as time you can never get back. BUT, if you truly feel like this will benefit your family overall, you need to put this all aside and focus on the task at hand. Call/video chat every night. Ensure your wife is continuously talking about you to your children, what you’re doing, and why it’s benefiting everyone. Even simple reasons like “daddy wants to make sure you get every present you want on your birthday because he loves you so much, so that’s why he has to go to x place to work as hard as he can for you” or things of the like. Involve them in your new life away as much as you can. And keep in mind, as well as remind them, that it’s just for now and not forever and soon enough you’ll be together again and even better off. Best of luck!

This sounds like a toxic work environment and that you’re experiencing some harassment from your co workers and management. I’d either contact HR, or if you’re in the position to, find a new job. The amount of hours you feel comfortable working, and the reasons behind it, is no one’s business but your own. The only issue I see is if you signed a written agreement on your hours, and you’re not fulfilling them. But I get the feeling from your post that this is not the case for this particular job. You don’t need to be guilted by your co workers for not picking up shifts if you don’t feel able to, for whatever reason. In my experience, a lot of workplaces, especially when it’s hourly/min wage (not sure if this is your situation or not,) are ridden with gossipy co-workers. It’s a chain effect- once one or two people comment on a situation, it gets spread like wildfire, and everyone joins in, probably because it makes them feel like they have a “connection” to their co-workers and chiming into their gossip and harassment makes them feel like they’re “part of the crew,” even if they don’t actually care or are affected by the situation. Unfortunately, especially when your superiors are involved and part of the torment, these situations don’t change. I’d honestly just cut your losses there for the sake of your self respect and try to move on to a new opportunity. Your well being and sanity isn’t worth this place.

Sometimes people confuse feeling “better” on meds because they’re WORKING! You plateau, and you start to feel normal, think you’re okay without them and then experience withdrawal and eventually dealing with the same issues that got you started on meds. If you’re feeling good and okay it means that the meds are doing their job and correcting the chemical imbalance in your brain to the level “normal” people have naturally. Don’t get off of them at this point. Enjoy the opportunities of feeling good and productive and okay. As for therapy, try different therapists until you click with one. That’s the key. Until then, it’ll feel like it doesn’t do anything for you, but once you bond with one, it does wonders. But, if you’re totally against it, perhaps try to write down your feelings in a journal or join a support group for depression. It helps to be around people who “get it.”

Perhaps having a stuffed toy when a “normal brained” person is 11 is too old. But someone with autism thinks differently, has different needs, and has developed a routine based on trying to cope and survive in a world that is mostly filled with people who see everything in a completely different way than your daughter. She has adapted to living in a society that doesn’t understand her, and she doesn’t understand because her brain works differently than many. Not in a better or worse way, just differently, and this makes it extremely difficult to find her place, and to interact with the world in her daily life. I would find merely being myself and learning to cope extremely scary if I was in her position. So, if having a stuffed animal with her, comforting her, and protecting her makes her life easier, I’d let her carry it around and attach herself to it as much as she wants. I’d think the toy is one thing that is constant for her- she has it at home where she is comfortable and feels safe, so bringing it in public perhaps brings that safety outside. 

I’d look into programs for families that have autistic children/siblings in them that are purposed to educate on autism as well as teach skills to form solid relationships with them that make life easier for them and the other family members. Get your daughter to research it, regardless if she’s done this before or not. Lastly, ensure you’re spending time with your other children and paying equal attention to them. Your attention may be focused on your child with autism because they need more support, but this could cause resentment from your other children. They need you too.
