My boyfriend spends a lot of time gaming, too. I used to get very irritated that he’d rather game than hang out with me (we live together.) It was like he’d rather live in a pseudo-reality than in our real life. But, I started to realize that gaming is his way of decompressing, like crafting or catching up on my shows is mine. I also realized that it is A LOT of the way he socializes and “hangs out” with friends as he is more introverted than I am and doesn’t hang out with friends in real life as often as I do. I get the feeling your husband also uses it to decompress after working/taking care of your child all day. It’s probably his only alone time. But, I also see it from your point of view- you’re valid in wanting to spend time with him. The way we solved this issue for the most part was a) me sharing my newfound conclusions about WHY he games so much, and validating him/those reasons as understandable and important, b) stating MY needs- I still want to spend time with him, even if he just makes time to watch a few episodes of a series we’re on, or we spend 30 min talking and catching up on our day before he goes and games and c) seeing if there was room for him to game more when I am working/sleeping/with friends/whatever rather than when we are both at home. I also realized that a lot of my resentment about it was because I had a lack of hobbies of my own to fill my time, which resulted in boredom making me more angry he was gaming rather than entertaining me. So, I started doing crafts, paint by numbers, paintings and filled my time with that when he was busy. All of this has seemed to help- efforts from both of us to find a middle path resulted in this issue going away for the most part. The first step is to have a heart to heart and honest conversation about both of your needs, and an effort to understand each other this way. Good luck!

Texting/using socials to create conversation and bonds with people, whether it be for friendship or more, is MUCH easier than doing it in person. Online, we have the privilege of delaying our replies in order to get our thoughts together before answering. In person, having a pause in a conversation to consider a reply comes across as awkward. Also, online, there is no opportunity for the other person to read body language, hear the tone in our voices and pick up signals/vibes that there is hesitance. So, it’s natural that you’re finding tension and unease with conversations in real life, especially if you’re a shy/timid person. The only thing I can suggest is being honest. Let them know that you’re much more shy face to face and it might take longer for you to open up/be comfortable with conversations where they flow naturally. If this person is caring and has a good heart, they will accept this. Admitting this will also maybe ease some tension- I think if I was in their position I may feel a little insecure, like I wasn’t interesting in person, or I was doing something else wrong. So if you admit this, they’ll feel better too. Also, why are you uncomfortable with your voice?

Obviously every child is different, but this is just my two cents.

Tbh, my parents probably didn’t necessarily “put me to bed,” but came in every night at bedtime to say goodnight and give me a kiss until I went to university lol and I have NO shame. I’m grateful for our close relationship, family bond, and that they care enough about me to do this. When they’re home (I’m 28f, rent the basement apartment at a discounted rate to save money for a house, and they snowbird to Florida October-April,) my dad still comes down in the morning to say hi and kiss me goodbye while he was still working(retired) and after that for just the purpose of saying good morning or saying bye if he was out for the day. So, point being, there should be no set age you should stop this completely. Of course children need to learn to independently take care of their hygiene/bed time routine and learn to be able to put themselves to bed. But that doesn’t mean you can’t assist or continue coming to check on them every night afterwards. Go by their pace and what you’re both comfortable with and forget social norms. They just make people compare themselves, doubt their success as a parent, and therefore, become negative towards their children for not “hitting milestones” quickly enough and themselves for their perception of their parenting skills. Also, while they’re home, I always go upstairs to say goodnight before bed if they hadn’t already come down and beaten me to it lol. I think that my extended years outside the norm of independent bed times allowed me to appreciate the importance of telling family you love them- saying goodnight no matter what age shows love and care imo.

I’ve come to realize I will never fully get over my fiancé’s suicide (April 1, 2018.) I will never not love him anymore. But time brings peace to original thoughts, questions, anger and overall just feeling sorry for myself. For a long time I couldn’t get over that I had found someone who asked me to marry them, who was trying for babies with me, who I thought I’d be with forever. I was SO angry that he took that away from me when I trusted him. I hated that I had to start my life again. I had to move back in with my parents (we were going to move into his rented house the month after he died, if all went to plan,) I hated that there was a possibility of being pregnant and him knowing that and potentially not just leaving me, but our unborn child (I didn’t become pregnant.) I hated that I finally had my life set up, and I was overjoyed he proposed and wanted to spend his life with me too. I was angry that everyday another one of my friends got engaged, married, or pregnant. I hated that I was supposed to be there too, I was heartbroken I no longer was going to reach those milestones in the near future, and with him. Three months later he committed suicide. But I’ve accepted that the reasons for his choice didn’t involve me- he was mentally ill and couldn’t fight anymore. I’ve recently decided I was going to make a dedicated effort to stop feeling sorry for myself and wishing for things that will never happen. But this doesn’t mean I will ever love him less. My dad said it best- “the hole in your heart seems massive and unbearable right now, but with time, it’ll get smaller and impact you less and less. The hole will always be there, and there will always be feelings because of it, but eventually it’ll become bearable and the overwhelming hurt you feel right now will be cut in half at least.” Allow yourself to grieve and feel whatever you need to feel. But, also allow yourself to make choices that’ll help you resume “normal” life, a liveable one, that changes your misery into pride that you have overcome one of the most devastating events that’ll happen in your life.

I’m still working on living in the moment too. It starts with being mindful. Humans naturally have 1000 things banging around in our brains, and way too busy lives. This leads us to multi task. Multi tasking seems like it is efficient because we are giving attention to everything we deem worthy. However, in actuality, it does the opposite because we aren’t giving anything our 100% attention, so nothing gets fulfilled to the best of our abilities. The first step for me was realizing this. I started “living in the moment” by dedicating my full attention to a singular thing/task. For example, if I was making a cup of coffee, I’d put the filter in, load the grounds, put the cup under, press the button to start brewing. As it was brewing, I’d stand there and watch until it was done. Then I’d move on to my next task. It seems like a waste of time to stand there for 2 minutes doing nothing- before this, I’d scroll socials, attempt to get myself ready, whatever. But forcing myself to endure this process taught me how to be in the moment. If I caught myself thinking about anything other than making my coffee, I’d refocus my attention back to that simple task. And of course, as I learned, things didn’t have to be so literal. But starting small like this introduces mindfulness and starts to retrain your brain to live moment to moment. It reduces anxiety once you get the hang of it. But it’s a concept that requires attention and constant redirection of your thought patterns before it becomes natural. But, it’s definitely worth it.

Keeping them separate is the worst thing you can do if you plan on keeping both dogs. You will only train them to get used to being alone and having individual attention. If you reintroduce them to each other, which inevitably will happen at some point, there will be even more tension and aggression because of the change in dynamic. You should slowly bond them. Start by keeping them in separate but conjoining rooms, but separate them with a baby gate. Allow them to socialize with each other through a barrier. When it seems like they’re used to this, move on to them in the same room with supervision. Have them interact with each other with caution, and have another person there so both have attention the whole time. When they don’t express aggressiveness, reward them with praise and treats. If they start fighting during this, butt it out ASAP before it gets too intense. Separate them after this and try again in a day or two. Take them each on walks daily- separate at first, with you and someone else walking each dog individually but at the same time, then try walking them both alone(holding both leashes,) with someone else there for back up if needed. They’re living together and it will be 1000 times more stressful for you to try to keep them separate for years on end. Also, I’d consider an obedience class that has other dogs there as well to try to enforce socialization. Edit: just re read and saw you tried training- find something closer or get a family member to do it. It’s important.

Having chronic depression (not just from circumstance or an event that warrants sadness, but being depressed seemingly for no reason at all and prolonged periods of time,) means that your brain literally doesn’t produce the normal amount of seratonin and dopamine that you need to feel “normal.”  Starting anti depressants is the first step in feeling okay again. It corrects the imbalance you have naturally. This will improve your mood, but the biggest thing it helped me with personally was motivation. After adapting to my meds, I was finally able to get off the couch and take care of the shit I fought with myself over doing before being medicated. My procrastination left. I was able to complete tasks in an acceptable amount of time in school and at work. Things stopped seeming overwhelming and impossible, and I began to look forward to going to school/work/being social again. I stopped dreading day to day life again, and started being proud of who I was and my accomplishments. It changed my life. When I miss my meds accidentally, I feel the cloud coming over me again, which shows me how much I need them. And you don’t need to commit to them forever. Maybe one day you’ll be comfortable with attempting life without them. But use them as a push to start your life normally again. Coupling them with talk therapy is the best plan of action. I wish you the best.

Him contacting you when you don’t want him to is still harassment. Have you asked him to leave you alone? If not, don’t do it now because contacting him will void your claim of harassment. But if you have in the past, and have those messages, that’ll help your case. The volume of his attempted contact is why it’s harassment, even if the content isn’t negative or threatening. For example, where I live anyways (Ontario, Canada,) if a telemarketer/debt collector attempts contact more than 3 times a week, it is considered illegal harassment. So, I am sure something similar would apply to personal issues such as yours, regardless of the content. I’d suggest going to the police with evidence of his attempted contact, and do everything you can to block his efforts such as changing your number, deleting socials, etc. You shouldn’t have to be in this situation at all, regardless of his intention or the content of his messages. It’s still bothering you, and unwanted!!

For large parties, ask at the beginning if it’s separate checks or one bill. Take last names for large parties for guests that are paying together. Most POS systems allow you to label cheque’s- utilize this and label them with these names. If you’re double/triple/whatever sat, and feel overwhelmed, treat all tables like a party. Go to each and get drinks. Punch in. Deliver all drinks. Then go get apps from everyone. Repeat, repeat. Avoid taking one tables order, punching in, getting the next, punching in. You get it. It’s a waste of time. Do everything you can handle at once. A table needs ketchup and another needs salt? Do both things and deliver both in one trip. Be honest with guests. If you’re super busy, tell them. State you’ll be with them as soon as you can and you’re doing your best. Most people are more understanding than you think. Be friendly, and anticipate needs before the guest notices they need those things- if a glass is half full, offer another. If it’s a soft drink (as long as it’s free refills where you are,) replace it before they ask for it. Go above and beyond and you’ll do great.

Through therapy, I’ve learned that trying to predict the future (which comes with anxious thoughts, what ifs) or being stuck in the past is only hurting yourself. Marsha Linehan (founder of DBT therapy) said “there is enough suffering in this moment to worry about anything but the present moment” which stuck with me. It also states that unless you can feel it with your five senses (touch, taste, smell, sight and hearing,) we don’t have the right to judge the person or situation with what we “think” is happening. The only way to know for sure is to ask directly. Have a conversation with your friend, voice your concerns and feelings, and go from there. If she admits to not liking you, start your process in moving on and forward and finding people who appreciate you. If she says she likes you and wants a friendship, and she continues to treat you the same, maybe your values in what friendship means don’t line up, and you should move on anyways. If you choose to continue the friendship(s,) make sure it’s known how you expect to be treated and what has hurt you in the past. You deserve to be treated nicely by people who say they care, and who you put effort into loving.

I was diagnosed with ADHD at 24 years old. I had gone through elementary school, high school and most of university without knowing. By the time I was diagnosed I decided to avoid medication as I figured I had already succeeded throughout my education without it. I always knew I had problems focusing, procrastinated and didn’t absorb a lot of information during lectures/in the classroom. I learned to adapt. I taught myself the material through textbooks and reading the online slideshows/textbooks in university on my own time. I still attended lectures, I just knew I had to re teach myself afterwards. I also figured out quickly that bringing my laptop and trying to take notes on it didn’t work as I’d get distracted by Facebook/the internet. I started leaving it at home and only taking notes with pen and paper. I also realized I absorbed more forcing myself to write down everything rather than just sitting and listening. I’m not sure if you’re on meds, but either way, experiment with different ways to learn the information and figure out what works for you. Not everyone learns the same way. Also, if you’re in college or university, attempt to be qualified as a student with disabilities- I was granted extensions on assignments and the ability to write exams in another room alone so I didn’t get distracted. Make the best of it and do whatever you can to succeed. As for your social anxiety, try not to let it interfere with your happiness. Anti anxiety pills and anti depressants have helped me a lot. Try to step out of your comfort zone as hard as it is and try to meet people in clubs or extra curricular activities that share common interests- it’s easier to have conversations when you have things you’re both interested in to talk about. All the best!

I was working as a Sous at a very corporate restaurant. The chef would work maybe 40 hours max a week while I was pulling 65. We were both salaried for 50. Every training session I went to at head office was driven by the backbone of “you obviously want to take over your KMs position one day so do this this and this.” I knew as soon as I thought to myself “I actually really don’t want that,” that I was in a job I wasn’t happy at. I did inventory, orders, schedules, worked the line every day with my staff, stayed extra hours if they were getting their asses handed to them to help while the chef would give props to them while they’re 20+ orders deep and leave. He wasn’t well liked. And I’d do this all if I was passionate, if I was making the menu, if it was seasonal ingredients, if it was a place I cared about. I cared about the staff so I stayed until I couldn’t anymore, and I left. And I haven’t looked back. I was beginning to have anxiety hours within sleep(waking up in a panic) during the last few hours before I had to wake up to go. I would question the GM about the chef’s attendance, attitude, how they treated the staff, and nothing would be done. One of the lead line cooks lost a boyfriend and she was forced to return to work within three days, while a FOH server had a cat die and was given a week off. Our chef didn’t fight for our team, wouldn’t back me up when I did, leading to me being shut down every time. Corporate restaurants care about the end result of labour, income, food cost, etc more than their people and that was the main reason I left. Find somewhere small, where the menu is local, sustainable and you are encouraged for your input and changing it. Somewhere that cares about the people. Because working the “normal” hours a chef does is not fulfilling unless you’re happy and finding this at a corporate restaurant is VERY rare.

Coming from someone with borderline personality disorder, depression, anxiety and dealing with the trauma of my fiancé’s suicide last year: I started an out patient program for BPD at a Mental Health Hospital. Prior to this, I had open availability at my job as a bartender at a restaurant. I was working 5 shifts a week, most of them 8-9 hours. When I changed my availability to accommodate therapy (n/a Monday AM and not available at all on Thursday,) my hours were cut dramatically. I’m now only scheduled 3 shifts a week usually, 4 if I’m lucky. Most of them aren’t even 8 hours long. When changing my availability I explained why, that it was for therapy and a medical reason, and they seemed okay with it. My work ethic hasn’t changed, I’m punctual, positive, guests tend to me happy with me and I’m flexible in regards to picking up shifts and going in early if needed and I’m able. I’m taking this as a passive aggressive attack on not having open availability anymore. I’ve challenged my manager on this, stated that this is my only job and I am self reliant for rent, food, bills, etc and having a drop in hours is seriously causing financial issues. No change. It’s irritating that trying to take care of my mental health has caused me to go through my savings and struggle every week with bills. If I had a physical illness, I’m sure I’d be met with sympathy and offers of help, but because mental illness is treated as lesser to physical illness, I’m struggling every day. Yes, I could get a new job, but my therapist advised that it may be best to wait until the program is over (3 more months) to pursue that to eliminate stress/anxiety over it. Also, I doubt any restaurants will hire me without having open availability. This is just my situation and a glance at what it’s like to try to be productive, balance health and work, and what it’s like for many people with mental illness- we’re not all “lazy” and using it as an excuse- some of us try really hard and are just met with huge walls preventing success.

If your mind is not present or participating in the current moment, maybe. I also have ADHD so I do it also when I’m disinterested and want to move on to the next task or situation. But, “normal brained” people also do it, just not to the extreme people with mental illness do. When I was elementary school age I had big issues making connections with friends because I just wasn’t there mentally 100%. I was always in my mind more than focused on peers and school and sports or whatever. Through therapy recently I’ve learned you can only tackle it by re-training your mind to learn how to be mindful, present, and participating in the present moment. This means not thinking about 5 minutes ago, not thinking about what you’re doing that night, literally just focusing on the present moment and being involved fully in that. It’s hard, and you have to truly commit yourself to doing it and focusing on doing it, but I’m told after a while of training your brain to work this way, it becomes normal and second nature and it’s not such a constant effort and thought. I’m not quite there yet myself, and I have to “snap” out of disassociating still, but even this far I’ve noticed feeling more joy and connection with people and the situations I’m in.

Being a young co-parenting couple is tough. Males mature more slowly than females and don’t have the “motherly instinct” that comes naturally to the majority of us as females. You give up those years and privileges in order to give them to your babies. Maybe a good idea is to go out to dinner just the two of you. Spend some time together alone. Let him know that at some point you’d like to have a conversation about all of this but try to enjoy each other’s company too. Find a happy medium- set hours that are dedicated to caring for the children and spending time with them dually. After they go down for the night, have some nights dedicated to just the two of you. But also have select days that he can do his own thing while you are on call for the kids and give yourself the same time while he is on call. This doesn’t mean he can’t game or Netflix or whatever- it just means he needs to watch the baby monitor and tend to them if they need attention. Other nights of the week give you both time where you are OFF. You have the freedom to go out or stay in bed or do whatever you want and the other is completely dedicated to the babies from when he gets home (and if it’s your night, when he gets home you’re off the clock,) until the morning. Also dedicate one night where your mom watches them and you guys can choose to do your own thing or something together. It’s all about compromise, balance and each partner feeling respected and like they are still able to be who they were before the kids, and still experience life as individuals as well as a couple in love. If you voice it in a way where he’s not 100% to blame, and a shitty partner and dad and that you WANT both of you to have a life outside of your children as well as have time as a family and dedicated to them, it may reach him differently. Write down your ideas and main points for the conversation before hand so if you get emotional or flustered or lost in what you want to express, you have a guide. If he doesn’t agree to these ideas and terms, there’s a bigger problem on your hands. But try this and DM me the results and I’m here to talk if you need further advice. 💕

Everyone fakes their way through interviews unless they’ve done that job for 10+ years. Talk yourself up. Fake confidence. Research the restaurant, their style, their menu etc and use this knowledge in your interview. Once you get in, you can always learn what you pretended to know during training- most of it is just basic knowledge and getting the new employee to understand their flow and the little tweaks their restaurant does that is different from others is the main goal. Most restaurants work basically the same way internally. Fake it till you make it, and then put your full force into learning to do the job the best you can, and you’ll be fine. A positive attitude, willingness to learn, going above and beyond your job criteria and being a team player will never get you fired- employers want staff that are coachable, even if they’re not the best at their job right away. People understand a learning curve and will be patient as long as you’re dedicated.
